analysis.one_liner: Ends billions in tax breaks, discounted royalties, and federal support for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would strip oil, gas, and coal companies of long-standing tax breaks and raise their federal royalty rate from 12.5% to 18.75%, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any action in the two years it had to move.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal dozens of special tax deductions and credits for oil, gas, and coal companies, raise the royalty they pay the government from 12.5% to 18.75% for drilling and mining on public land, end taxpayer-funded fossil fuel research and loan guarantees, block export agencies from financing overseas fossil fuel projects, and remove the legal limit on how much companies must pay after an offshore oil spill. It died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit through cleaner air and water, a reduced federal deficit as industry tax breaks end, more revenue from public-land energy, and coal miners' benefits funded permanently. Communities near pipelines, offshore rigs, and mines benefit from unlimited corporate liability for spills and contamination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, coal miners, and communities near polluting sites

how_it_helps.text: It repeals a long list of special tax rules available only or mainly to fossil fuel companies, including percentage depletion, intangible drilling cost expensing, last-in first-out inventory accounting, and the corporate income tax exemption for publicly traded fossil fuel partnerships [S2][S3].

It raises the royalty rate companies pay for oil, gas, and coal taken from federal land from 12.5% to 18.75%, and bars royalty relief on future offshore leases, so taxpayers get closer to market value for public resources [S2][S3].

It removes the statutory cap on offshore facility and pipeline operator liability under the Oil Pollution Act, so companies pay the full cost of spills they cause, and it denies tax deductions for oil spill cleanup and damages [S2][S3].

It ends the Department of Energy's Fossil Energy Research and Development Program, bars federal financing agencies and international institutions from supporting fossil fuel projects, and terminates fossil fuel research tax credits, saving public money and ending direct federal support for the industry [S2][S3].
It makes the excise tax funding the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund permanent at a higher rate, so miners' benefits are not paid from general taxpayer funds when the temporary rate lapses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies bear the direct cost: they lose tax breaks worth billions per year, pay higher royalties, face a new 13% excise tax on Gulf of Mexico production, and must cover full spill liability. Some of these costs would be passed to consumers in the form of somewhat higher energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies, partly via higher energy prices

drawbacks.text: Higher taxes, royalties, and a new 13% excise tax on Gulf of Mexico crude would raise production costs, and energy companies would pass some of that on to consumers through higher fuel and electricity prices [S2][S3].

The bill terminates the carbon oxide sequestration credit (section 45Q) even for carbon capture that is unrelated to producing more oil, which supporters of carbon capture would view as cutting off a tool for reducing emissions [S3].

Ending federal fossil fuel research, loan guarantees, and export financing immediately could disrupt projects and jobs in coal and oil regions, and raising royalties may make some federal-land production uneconomical, reducing domestic supply [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a broad, deliberate removal of special treatment for one industry, and its benefits to taxpayers, public revenue, and accountability for spills are real and large. The honest cost is that some of it shows up at the pump and on utility bills, and it eliminates the 45Q carbon capture credit entirely rather than reforming it. On balance, ending subsidies to a mature, profitable industry while keeping the Black Lung fund solvent weighs in favor of the bill's aims, but the energy-price and carbon-capture objections are legitimate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2021 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on April 15, 2021 with five original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S3][S5].
Eight Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the referral to the Finance Committee: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress [S5][S1].
The CRS summary describes the bill as limiting or eliminating fossil fuel subsidies through royalty, liability, research, and tax changes [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which kept their tax deductions, the 12.5% royalty rate, liability caps, and federal research and financing support for the entire two-year Congress and beyond.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act of 2021 and recruited five original cosponsors.

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Merkley, Markey, Booker, Van Hollen, and Warren.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry (oil, gas, and coal companies)
against.role: Beneficiaries of the subsidies the bill repeals
against.what_they_did: Fought to preserve fossil fuel tax breaks and royalty terms, which the industry has long lobbied to keep.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Democrats or independents aligned with Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where each party stood.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill repeals their special deductions and credits, raises the federal royalty rate from 12.5% to 18.75%, imposes a 13% excise tax on Gulf of Mexico production, and removes liability caps for spills. The industry's gain from keeping these rules comes directly at the public's expense through lost revenue, subsidies, and unpaid spill costs.

The bill repeals percentage depletion and capital gains treatment for coal royalties, ends the refined coal credit, and raises royalties for federal coal leases. The coal industry's interest in keeping these breaks runs against the taxpayers who fund them and against public health.

The bill strips the CERCLA exemption that shields big lenders (banks over $10 billion in assets and investment firms over $250 billion) from liability for environmental cleanup at sites they finance, meaning they would bear pollution costs they are currently insulated from.
The bill repeals the corporate income tax exemption for publicly traded partnerships earning fossil fuel income, ending a structure that saves these entities corporate taxes.

industries.industry: Coal miners and the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund
industries.note: A permanent, higher excise tax on coal funds miners' black lung benefits, so the fund is not left short and paid from general revenues.
